questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes a "deployable" agent a stricter bar than a "working" one built and tested in Lessons 29-30?
options: A deployable agent needs entirely different tool schemas than the working build
A deployable agent has to behave correctly when no one is watching it run, which is a different and stricter requirement than working correctly while a developer observes each run
There is no real difference; working and deployable mean exactly the same thing
Deployable agents cannot use any of the controls built in Lesson 30
questions.explain: The lesson draws a clear line: a build that works under direct observation isn't automatically safe unattended, which is the actual bar deployment has to clear.

questions.q: Why does an in-memory audit log, which works fine during local testing, become a problem in a deployed system?
options: In-memory logs are always faster and therefore always preferred
It disappears the moment the service restarts, losing the durable record that Lesson 21 established an audit log needs to be
In-memory logs cannot record tool_use_id values
The Claude API forbids in-memory logging
questions.explain: An in-memory list vanishes on restart, which directly undermines the append-only, durable record-keeping that Lesson 21 established as the whole point of an audit log.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say a hardcoded budget or iteration limit is a problem for deployment, even though it worked fine while developing?
options: Hardcoded values run slower than values loaded from config
It can't be adjusted without shipping a new code deploy, unlike a value read from configuration, which is a meaningful difference once the agent is running as a live service
The Claude API does not allow hardcoded numeric values
Hardcoded budgets are illegal under data privacy regulations
questions.explain: A config-driven budget can be tuned without a redeploy; a hardcoded one requires a full code change and release just to adjust a number, which is impractical for a live service.

questions.q: Why does Lesson 27's monitoring only become meaningful at the deployment stage, according to this lesson?
options: Monitoring is irrelevant once an agent is deployed

During development, a developer watches every run directly; in deployment, no one is watching individual runs, so the aggregate signals (rejection rate, limit trips, cost trend) become what a team actually relies on
Monitoring can only be configured after the agent is permanently shut down
Lesson 27's signals require a feature that doesn't exist until the next course
questions.explain: Monitoring's aggregate signals only have something continuous to describe once there's a deployed system running unattended — during development, direct observation already served that purpose.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is intentionally left out of the capstone, to be covered in the next course in the AI Engineer path?
options: Tool schema design, which was never covered in this course
Approval checkpoints, which are left entirely unbuilt
Real infrastructure choices — which cloud, which secrets manager, how to provision the sandbox as actual infrastructure, how to wire real alerting
Audit logging, which is deferred to a future course
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly scopes out concrete infrastructure decisions as their own subject, naming Azure AI & Cloud for AI Engineers as the next course that picks up deployment, security, and monitoring in a real cloud environment.
